title: The Motivation Fractal
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane argues that the most reliable classroom-wide motivation strategy isn't tailoring content to individual interests -- which is logistically impossible across a full class of different students -- but engineering a felt sense of success, since humans are motivated by doing things they feel good at. He introduces the 'motivation fractal' as a mental model: within a single activity, difficulty should start easy and gradually increase; the same pattern repeats within a class period across its component activities, within a topic across its classes, and arguably within a whole year of school. Each new unit of time should start noticeably easier than where the previous one ended, building momentum before ramping challenge back up. Kane is explicit that this is only a mental model, not something he can execute with perfect consistency given the practical realities of teaching, but he treats it as his single most effective tool for keeping a diverse class of students with different needs, knowledge levels, and interests broadly motivated at once.
points: Kane's core claim reorders the usual motivation advice: rather than chasing individual relevance for each student, he treats felt success (a shared, engineerable experience) as the more scalable motivational lever for a whole class.

The 'fractal' framing -- the same easy-to-hard ramp repeating at the scale of an activity, a class, a topic, and a year -- gives teachers a single mental model applicable at multiple planning grain sizes.

Kane explicitly ties this to hard-problem avoidance: students who say 'I don't know' and give up on tough problems are, in his account, better served by a run-up of easier problems than by direct exhortation to try harder.

He's careful to flag the model's limits -- it can't fully account for the wide range of individual needs (language learners, IEPs, students with anxieties) in a real class, and practical logistics prevent perfect execution every day.
quotes: In my experience, the best motivation strategy is simple. Humans like doing things we feel good at. I want students to feel successful in math class.
Math teachers often complain that students aren't willing to try hard problems. They look at a problem, say "I don't know," and give up.
The best answer I've found is to help students feel successful before trying a hard problem. Build up to it with a few easier, more accessible problems. Use success to build momentum.
Within each activity, the difficulty gradually increases, starting easier and getting more difficult.
When I see motivation flagging, I try to build in a more gradual increase in difficulty in the activity, or class, or topic.
when I do a good job of starting small and gradually increasing the difficulty, building confidence as we go, I can see slow, steady progress in motivating my students.
